sources.title: 8 ways to make school morning routines easier
sources.quote: Check that all books, homework, and changes of clothing are packed up and by the door. ... Then, ask your child to pick out an outfit for the next day. ... Try not to be racing around to get yourself ready at the same time. ... Set your child’s alarm to play a favorite song. ... Make every day as predictable as you can. ... Designate spots for school supplies, sports gear, coats, and jackets. ... By making time more visible, you’ll help teach your child how to manage time. ... Give manageable countdowns, like “At 7:25, it’ll be time to put your shoes on.” ... Have your child check and re-check to make sure everything’s packed before leaving the house. ... This is a simple way to help your child get the most out of a smoother morning.
sources.supports: School morning routine tips: prepare the night before, let the child choose the outfit, parents ready before the child, a favorite song as the alarm, a predictable routine, fixed spots for gear, visible time and countdowns, a double check at the door and a small reward. A parenting page for families of school age children, used as general advice; no promise of a result.

sources.title: How to Help Kids Learn to Fail
sources.quote: It's hard, but parents need to try step back and give kids room to mess up. ... If you're always over their shoulder guiding them, they can't fail and try again. ... I see you're really disappointed, I know you really wanted to do better. ... When your kid is ready, talk about what went wrong and how they might do things differently next time. ... You can also talk about your own mistakes or failures.
sources.supports: Step back and give room to try again, name the child's disappointment first, talk about what to change later when the child is ready, and share your own mistakes. Applied to a child who gives up fast as general advice.

sources.title: How Can We Help Kids With Self-Regulation?
sources.quote: If a parent hovers too much, they risk taking over the regulation role. ... Scaffolding in this situation might be helping the child with one problem, and then expecting them to try the rest. ... They might use a timer to give themselves periodic breaks.
sources.supports: Help with one problem and expect the child to try the rest, do not hover, and use a timer for breaks. General advice about frustration and self-regulation.

sources.title: Frustration...and Persistence
sources.publisher: SDPB, South Dakota Public Broadcasting (9 Sep 2021)
sources.quote: Help your child find a way of calming down that works: taking some belly breaths, counting to 10, or taking a break. ... Encourage her to walk away and try again later. ... Break the task into lots of little steps. ... Remind him that it's not that he can't do it—it's that he can't do it…yet!
sources.supports: A calming tool (belly breaths, counting to 10, a break), walking away and trying again later, small steps, and the word yet. A public media parenting page, general advice, no promise of a result.

sources.title: Frustration Tolerance
sources.quote: When they fall apart, let them know that you appreciate how difficult it can be ... 'stretching' activities that are difficult but achievable can be enriching and expand their learning.
sources.supports: Tell a frustrated child you see how hard it is, and choose activities that are difficult but achievable. A page about toddlers, applied to a school age child by analogy.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.quote: Read stories about feelings.
sources.supports: Reading stories about feelings is one of the ways Zero To Three suggests to help a child with big feelings. The page is about empathy, used only as support for reading stories about a hard moment.
